title: Arb Finder: A Free Sports-Betting Arbitrage Web App
text:
The question
Sportsbooks price the same games independently. When two books disagree by enough, betting every outcome at the best available prices pays back more than it costs, whichever side wins. That’s an arbitrage. Tools that find these usually charge a monthly subscription. I wanted to build one that anyone can use for free, that costs nothing to run, and that explains the math and the risks honestly.

title: Arb Finder: A Free Sports-Betting Arbitrage Web App
Arb Finder: A Free Sports-Betting Arbitrage Web App
text:
What I learned

Odds are probabilities, and that one idea does most of the work. Converting prices to implied probabilities turns a book’s margin and an arbitrage into the same calculation, run in opposite directions. The app uses it both to find arbs and to price cover bets.
The hard part isn’t the formula. It’s making sure two prices are really the same bet. Most of the engine’s logic is about matching identical outcomes across books and discarding stale or one-sided lines, because a false arb costs a user real money.
Costs shape the design. The API bills per sport for game lines but per game for props. That drove the up-front credit estimate, defaults that keep each request at one credit per market, and caching so that re-filtering results is free.
Releasing something publicly means checking more than the code: data licensing, platform rules, state-by-state legality, and responsible-gambling messaging.




Game-line results with sample data: each card shows the arbitrage, where to place each side, and how much to stake





Player-prop mode: same player, same stat, same line, matched across two books


Tools: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML, CSS, The Odds API (REST, v4), headless Chrome for automated testing, Git/GitHub, GitHub Pages.

title: Competitive Fortnite: Prize Pools, Engagement and Regional Fairness
text:
The question
Fortnite’s developer, Epic Games, runs one of the largest competitive gaming circuits in the world. I asked four questions about it: Does prize money move with public interest in the game? Do major tournaments draw more attention? As prize money changed, did more players earn a share or did it concentrate at the top? And is prize money split between world regions in proportion to how many people play there?

title: Competitive Fortnite: Prize Pools, Engagement and Regional Fairness
text:
What I did

Collected the data myself from seven sources: $209.1M of prize money across 2,674 tournaments and 11,443 players, 113 months of Twitch viewership, weekly Google search interest, World Bank and Census data, and 26 seasons of regional championship prize pools. Every request followed each site’s rules on automated access, with delays between requests.
Validated everything. Automated checks reconcile my totals with the source’s own published figures. They caught a $2.0M event missing from the source’s listings and multi-game events that would have double counted money.
Analysed it four ways: time series comparisons (in levels and in changes, to avoid spurious correlation), an event study with season controls and Newey-West standard errors, inequality measures (Gini coefficients, Lorenz curves, top-N shares), and a regional allocation analysis tested under three different player-base proxies.
Wrote it up as a reproducible Quarto report that explains the game and every method for non-specialist readers, with the code folded under each result.

title: Competitive Fortnite: Prize Pools, Engagement and Regional Fairness
text:
What I found

Prize money and public attention follow different paths: viewership and search interest fell steadily after 2018 while prize money held up until 2024, and month-to-month changes are essentially uncorrelated.
Tournaments barely move mainstream attention (about +3% in a finals week) compared with new game seasons (about +28%).
From 2019 to 2025 prize money fell 84% while the number of players earning anything fell only 32%, and the top 100 earners’ share rose from 44% to 65%.
A common belief among players, that Europe is underpaid relative to North America Central, is not supported: Europe receives 1.14x its share of players and NA Central 0.99x. The largest gaps are in smaller regions.




Prize share vs. player share by region, 2025-2026





Prize money vs. attention, indexed to 2018


Tools: R (tidyverse, httr2, rvest, gtrendsR, sandwich, ineq), Quarto, Git/GitHub.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index: NBA Scoring, Skill vs. the Whistle
text:
The question
“Ethical hooper” is basketball slang for a player who scores through pure skill (clean footwork, natural shot-making, smooth handles) rather than foul-baiting, flopping, or jumping into defenders to draw a whistle. I wanted to know whether that idea could be measured. Who are the most and least “ethical” scorers since 1996-97? And when the NBA told referees in 2021-22 to stop rewarding “non-basketball moves,” did it hit the players my index had flagged?

title: The Ethical Hooper Index: NBA Scoring, Skill vs. the Whistle
text:
What I did

Built the dataset from 30 seasons of NBA play-by-play and shot charts (1996-97 to 2025-26, regular season and playoffs): 6.3 million shots and every foul and free throw, linked to official minutes and positions from Basketball Reference.
Validated it against independent sources. My counts of shooting fouls drawn, and-ones, offensive fouls and assisted shots match Basketball Reference’s own tables (correlations of 0.998 or higher), and attempts, free throws and turnovers match official totals within ±2 for every 1,000-minute season. The checks also caught real problems: 16 games missing from the source archive, a 2025-26 change in how the NBA logs end-of-quarter heaves, and Hall of Famers’ playoff seasons filed under a different name.
Trained an expected-field-goal model (xgboost) on shot location, distance, shot type, game clock and season, but never on who took the shot. It beat a zone-average baseline on a held-out season (log-loss 0.639 vs. 0.657) and is closely calibrated.
Designed the index from eight components on two axes. Skill: shot-making above expected, self-created makes, shot difficulty and clean footwork. Whistle: free throws beyond what a player’s shot diet predicts, three-point fouls drawn, free-throw share of points, and and-ones on jumpers. I used empirical-Bayes shrinkage so small samples don’t create fake extremes, and standardized everything within season so eras compare fairly.
Ran a difference-in-differences and event study of the 2021-22 rule change, with a placebo rule date and a separate treatment window to rule out regression to the mean.
Published it as an eight-page Quarto website with searchable rankings and an interactive player lookup.

title: The Ethical Hooper Index: NBA Scoring, Skill vs. the Whistle
text:
What I found

Steve Nash is the most ethical hooper of the last 30 years (career score 87.7 out of 100), followed by Payton Pritchard, Ish Smith, Nikola Vučević and Chris Paul. James Harden ranks last of 417 qualifying careers (10.7).
The style is a real, lasting trait: a player’s score correlates 0.74 with the next season’s, and the rankings barely change under alternative weightings (rank correlations of 0.89 to 0.99).
The crackdown worked league-wide: three-point shooting fouls fell from 1.42 to 1.08 per 100 attempts in one season. The apparent extra drop for prior foul-drawers turned out to be mostly regression to the mean, since a fake “placebo” rule date shows a similar decline.
But the index predicted who lost efficiency: players with higher pre-rule Whistle Scores lost 0.38 points of true shooting per standard deviation afterward (p = 0.049), while the placebo showed nothing (p = 0.81).




The Ethical Hooper map: every qualifying career, Skill Score vs. Whistle Score





Foul-drawers lost efficiency after the 2021-22 crackdown


Tools: R (data.table, arrow, xgboost, fixest, ggplot2, gt, reactable), Quarto with Observable JS, renv, Git/GitHub.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector: Which Decisions Did the Stats Say Went the Wrong Way?
text: Read the full report Browse the leaderboard View the code on GitHub

title: The UFC Robbery Detector: Which Decisions Did the Stats Say Went the Wrong Way?
text:
The question
Every fight fan has a list of “robberies”: decisions they’re sure went to the wrong fighter. I wanted to test that claim with data. Given what actually happened in each round (strikes, knockdowns, takedowns, control time), how likely was the declared winner to get the decision from real judges? I call one minus that probability the Robbery Score. It measures disagreement between the statistics and the result. It is never an accusation of judge misconduct, because statistics can’t see everything judges can.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector: Which Decisions Did the Stats Say Went the Wrong Way?
text:
What I did

Built and linked three data sources:

round-by-round statistics for every UFC fight, from UFCStats;
every judge’s round-by-round scorecard plus 51,355 media scorecards, from MMADecisions, collected with the site owner’s permission;
historical betting lines from BestFightOdds.

All 4,109 decisions from 2001 to November 2026 were linked across the sources. I checked the robots.txt and terms of every site, paused between requests and cached every page.
Found and fixed two data problems before reporting anything:

Point deductions: MMADecisions round scores already include them, so a 10-9 round with a point taken away looked like a 9-9 “draw” (109 deductions in 105 fights).
Fighter order: UFCStats lists the winner first, not the red corner, for fights before March 2010.

Trained a round model on 33,444 real judge round scores. It predicts which fighter a judge gives each round from that round’s statistics alone. Training rounds were mirrored so the model can’t learn “the red corner wins”. I compared logistic regression, glmnet and xgboost (tidymodels) with grouped cross-validation by fight and a 2020–2026 time-based test. Every model cut log-loss by about 30% against a “whoever landed more strikes wins” baseline (0.38 vs. 0.55).
Simulated 10,000 sets of three correlated judges for every fight.

The correlation between judges was estimated by maximum likelihood. It reproduces how often real judges split on a round: 22.0% observed vs. 22.2% predicted, where independent judges would split 35.9% of the time.
The simulation also models 10-8 rounds, 10-10 rounds and point deductions.
It uses out-of-fold predictions, so no fight’s own scorecards inform its own score.

Validated the score against independent evidence: media scorecards the model never sees, a hand-picked list of widely debated decisions, calibration checks, and a sensitivity test with a different model (rank correlation 0.987).
Studied the judges with mixed models that have judge random effects. I estimated red-corner and betting-favourite effects, and tested whether the 2017 Unified Rules scoring criteria changed what judges reward.
Published it as a seven-page Quarto website with a searchable leaderboard and round-by-round breakdowns of featured fights. The whole thing is a reproducible targets pipeline with renv-pinned packages, and no number in the write-up is typed by hand.

title: The UFC Robbery Detector: Which Decisions Did the Stats Say Went the Wrong Way?
text:
What I found

About 1 in 18 decisions is a statistical “robbery”. 225 of 4,049 decisions (5.6%) have a Robbery Score of at least 0.75. The highest scores belong to Igor Pokrajac vs. Fabio Maldonado (2012) and Leonard Garcia vs. Nam Phan (2010).
The score lines up with people who watched the fights. It correlates with the share of media scoring the fight for the loser at r = 0.59. The stats-only model agrees with the media majority 87.7% of the time, close to the official result’s 89.8%. 11 of 13 widely debated decisions rank in the top 16%.
What judges reward, measured in significant head strikes:

a knockdown is worth about 12;
a submission attempt about 5;
a minute of control about 3;
a takedown about 2;
a failed takedown attempt costs about 0.7.

Judges lean slightly toward the red corner and the betting favourite. On a round the stats call 50/50, the red corner gets about 4.7 points more, and a −300 favourite about 6.5 points more. Adjusted for how hard their fights were to score, individual judges agree with the stats at very similar rates.
The 2017 criteria changed what judges reward, but not how often decisions go “wrong”. A knockdown rose from about 9 to 15 head strikes and a takedown fell from 2.7 to 1.9 (joint test p = 0.0006). The Robbery-tier rate showed no clear change.




Round-by-round breakdown of the decision with the highest Robbery Score





What judges reward: each statistic’s value in significant head strikes





The Robbery Score against media scorecards


Tools: R (targets, tidymodels, xgboost, glmnet, lme4, sandwich, shapviz, rvest/httr2, arrow, ggplot2, patchwork, gt, reactable), Quarto, renv, Git/GitHub.
